query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The preservation of structural and chemical stability in near‐equiatomic multi‐element nanoparticles under high‐temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions is governed by the selective formation of a self-passivating oxide layer—originating from specific reactive elements (e.g., chromium) present in the alloy—which, in combination with high configurational entropy that slows atomic diffusion, suppresses sintering and phase separation.
generation.material_initial_state: Near‐equiatomic, chemically homogeneous solid‐solution nanoparticles (HEA-type) without a preformed oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled doping of a reactive element (for example, adding ~5 atom% Cr) to the nanoparticle composition that is known to preferentially oxidize and form a protective oxide (e.g., Cr2O3).
generation.conditions: Exposure to service regimes typical of catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K in an oxidizing or reactive environment.
generation.structural_mediator: The in situ formation of a uniform, self-healing oxide shell (such as Cr2O3) at the nanoparticle surface.
generation.mechanism: The reactive dopant oxidizes preferentially at high temperatures, creating a protective oxide barrier that reduces further oxidation and atomic diffusion. This barrier, coupled with the high configurational entropy of the solid solution structure, minimizes sintering and phase separation, thereby preserving both the structural integrity and chemical composition of the nanoparticles.
generation.predicted_outcome: Doped nanoparticles (with Cr) will demonstrate significantly reduced sintering and phase changes (i.e., more preserved nanoparticle size and homogeneous phase) compared to undoped nanoparticles, as evidenced by a stable protective oxide layer formation during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
generation.baseline: Undoped near‐equiatomic nanoparticles that lack the reactive element are expected to show more pronounced nanoparticle coarsening, phase separation, or compositional degradation under the same conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to multi-element, near‐equiatomic nanoparticles whose initial structure is a solid solution; it is valid in environments where the thermodynamics favor protective oxide formation (i.e., sufficient oxygen activity and appropriate service temperature ranges). It may not hold for systems where either the alloy composition or external conditions prevent oxide formation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise threshold concentration of the reactive dopant required for optimal passivation and the kinetics of oxide layer formation under different service atmospheres are not fully established. Additionally, the interplay between nanoparticle size, composition, and oxide stability may introduce variability in the observed effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of near‐equiatomic nanoparticles: one group doped with approximately 5 atom% Cr and another identical set without any intentional doping. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature conditions representative of catalytic and thermoelectric service regimes in an oxidizing atmosphere. Periodically analyze the samples using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for morphological changes, X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase stability, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) for the presence and composition of surface oxides.
measurements: Particle size distribution and morphology (via TEM)
Phase composition and crystallographic structure (via XRD)
Surface chemistry and oxide layer identification (via XPS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cr-doped nanoparticles do not exhibit a consistently thicker or more protective oxide shell and if they do not show reduced sintering, phase separation, or compositional degradation relative to the undoped baseline under the same conditions, the hypothesis that selective oxide formation governs enhanced stability will be deemed falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

Development of materials suitable for molten fluoride salt environments started in the 1950s with the Aircraft Reactor Experiment (ARE) [4] . This experiment used Inconel 6
